title: Κάμηλος ὀρχουμένη
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 147. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κάμηλος ἀναγκαζομένη ὑπὸ τοῦ ἰδίου δεσπότου ὀρχήσασθαι εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’ οὐ μόνον ὀρχουμένη εἰμὶ ἄσχημος, ἀλλὰ καὶ περιπατοῦσα. »
sentences.tr: Kamēlos anankazomenē hypo tou idiou despotou orchēsasthai eipen· « All’ ou monon orchoumenē eimi aschēmos, alla kai peripatousa. »
sentences.l: A camel, being compelled by her own master to dance, said: « But not only when dancing am I ungainly, but when walking about as well. »
sentences.n: ἄσχημος is "without shape", ill-made to look at. The two participles ὀρχουμένη and περιπατοῦσα name the occasions on which the ugliness shows, and the joke lies in the camel conceding the charge and enlarging it. ἀλλά at the head of a reply registers an objection, "come now".

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος εἴρηται ἐν παντὶ ἔργῳ ἀπρέπειαν ἔχοντι.
sentences.tr: Ho logos eirētai en panti ergōi aprepeian echonti.
sentences.l: The story has been spoken in the case of every deed that has unseemliness in it.
sentences.n: εἴρηται is the perfect passive of the old verb whose forms fill out λέγω, "it has been spoken". ἐν with the dative marks the case to which the story is applied rather than a place. ἀπρέπεια is the quality of not being fitting — of a thing that will look wrong however it is done.
